newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: WTO cites concern on Canadian reliance on US trade.
newsitem.headline: WTO cites concern on Canadian reliance on US trade.

text.p: Canada's gradual economic and trade liberalisation has boosted the economy, but concerns persist about its high reliance on trade with the United States, a report by the World Trade Organisation (WTO) said on Tuesday.

Domestic and external reforms had touched virtually all sectors of Canada's export-driven economy, except for a few "sensitive" areas still enjoying protection such as cultural industries and supply-managed agriculture, the report said.
Trade delegates from 125 member states were to wind up a two-day debate on the report by WTO economists later in the day.
The 137-page study concluded that Canada's overall trade policies remained "firmly anchored in the WTO", but added:
"After decades of North American market integration, starting with the Auto Pact in 1965, most sectors are now exposed to, and perform well in, full competition with their U.S. counterparts.

"Concerns persist, however, about the potential vulnerability of the Canadian economy deriving from such high reliance on one large trading partner, on a handful of traditional industries and on relatively few large-scale plants," it added.
European and Asian nations were expected to challenge aspects of the North America Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA), including possible trade diversion, according to trade sources.
Exports and investment have been behind strengthening Canada's economy since early 1994, according to the report.

"Both 'traditional' industries such as minerals, lumber and automobiles, and 'advanced' sectors have benefited from strong demand in the United States, currency depreciation vis-a-vis the U.S. dollar and liberalisation under NAFTA and the WTO.
"During the period, the United States' share in Canada's trade has continued to rise, currently accounting for four-fifths of merchandise exports and two-thirds of imports."
Bilateral tariff reductions under NAFTA have intensified North American market integration, according to the WTO report.
Canada's tariffs on U.S.-made manufactures currently average only about one per cent (as against 6.6. per cent on imports on a most-favoured-nation basis), it said.
More than 58 per cent of all tariff lines carry zero rates for U.S. supplies, with full bilateral tariff elimination, except for certain farm items scheduled for 1998.

Canadian federal expenditure on agriculture has been reduced by some 20 per cent since 1994, mainly through elimination of grain transport subsidies, according to WTO. The impact of such cuts has been offset by strong export growth.
"The more market-based environment for grains and major livestock industries contrasts, however, with the retention of supply management regimes for dairy products, poultry and eggs."

"These products continue to be sheltered by high import barriers, now in the form of restrictive tariff quotas with excess supplies carrying prohibitive rates, ranging up to over 300 per cent for butter," the report said. Historical monopolies remain in areas such as butter, condensed and concentrated milk.
Regarding manufacturing, the WTO report said that U.S.-based companies currently accounted for 90 per cent of all cars and 60 per cent of all computers produced in Canada.

Large foreign-owned plants are complemented by a network of small and medium-sized Canadian firms, including producers of technically advanced niche products in such areas as information technologies and aviation, according to the report.
On Canadian services, the WTO report said that there was a general climate of deregulation, privatisation and management reform. This was also stimulated by competitive U.S. pressures.
Competition has been introduced in the telecommunications industry, and domestic air transport has been liberalised.

Canada gives significant aid via direct subsidies, tax incentives, local-content requirements and foreign-ownership restrictions to cultural activities (visual and performing arts, publishing, music,film, and CD-Rom). The sector employs 670,000 and has an annual revenue of $16 billion Canadian dollars.
